name: Erik Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Larkfield Eggs, sixteen thousand free-range hens in four sheds, owned by Tom and Sarah Whitlock. I'm in at half six to check the sheds, then it's collecting and grading eggs, which means sorting them by size and checking for cracks, until about eleven. Afternoons I walk the ranges, pick up any birds that have died, fix the electric fence, and at dusk I make sure every pop-hole, the little doors the hens go in and out of, is shut against the fox.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the egg farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a hardware shop on Station Road for twenty-six years. Nails by the pound, keys cut while you wait. The big DIY place opened on the ring road and people started ordering online, and at fifty-four I sold the stock and shut the door. Tom Whitlock was a customer, and he asked if I'd like a job where nobody asks for a refund.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine and I like being trusted with the place at dusk, when it's just me and the hens settling. What wears me out is the dead birds, and not knowing why. Sarah can look at a hen and tell you it's got worms or a bad egg stuck, and I'm still learning which ones to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't need it and I don't want it. People got along without it before. If Tom wants to use it for his paperwork, that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me. I've never used one and I don't intend to. My grandson tried to show me on his phone at Easter and I told him to put it away at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Margaret, my wife, and I have about three months' money put by, and that stays. I'd like to get better at spotting a sick hen before Sarah does, just once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's nothing to do with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people got along without it. Is that how you felt about the internet, when the shop was going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose it is. I didn't blame the internet so much as people. They'd come in, ask my advice for twenty minutes, then go home and order it cheaper online. I never said a word, but I remember every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting it right before Sarah mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean I'm not just a pair of hands. At the shop, people came to me because I knew things. Here I'm the new man at fifty-eight, and that takes some swallowing.

S0.say: I'd say I don't need it and don't want it, because people got along without it. If Tom uses it for paperwork, that's his business.
S0.think: I think it doesn't touch me, and I've never used one. When my grandson tried to show me at Easter, I told him to put it away at the table.
S0.do: Carries on as before with about three months of savings left alone. Tries to get better at spotting a sick hen before Sarah does.
S0.feel: Calm; it has nothing to do with him.
S0.quote: They'd come in, ask my advice for twenty minutes, then go home and order it cheaper online.
S0.fieldNote: Erik doesn't blame the technology for his shop closing; he blames customers who took his advice and bought elsewhere. Being the new man at fifty-eight costs him some pride. He's firm and courteous at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame about the youngsters. The answer is apprenticeships, proper ones, where a young person learns from an old hand. Not more college courses that end in nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a beginner who got a chance because Tom knew me. Fewer beginners hired means fewer young men getting that chance, and that's how communities go downhill. Idle young men get into trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the vicar about the youth club, see if some of the lads could come up to Larkfield on Saturdays and help. I'd ask Tom if he'd take one on properly. And I'd keep my head down and do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad from the youth club, Callum, sixteen, his dad left and his mum works nights. He's got good hands, he fixed the church boiler with me last winter. If nobody takes a lad like that on, he'll drift, and it won't be his fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with handouts, no. If they want to help, they can make it easier for a small farm to take on an apprentice, less paperwork, a bit of money for the training. Tom told me he gave up on it last time because of the forms.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for the youngsters, and the answer is proper apprenticeships with old hands. Not more college courses that end in nothing.
S1.think: I think fewer beginners means fewer young men getting the chance Tom gave me. That's how communities go downhill, because idle young men get into trouble.
S1.do: Asks the vicar about bringing youth club lads to the farm on Saturdays and asks Tom to take one on properly. Keeps his head down at work.
S1.quote: He's got good hands, he fixed the church boiler with me last winter.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional values come through as a duty to young men in his community, not as a lecture. He has a specific lad in mind, Callum, and a practical plan through the church. He wants government help as less paperwork, not as money handed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of fuss from people who sit at desks. Working people have been through this before, in mills and mines, and nobody marched for them. If office workers need to retrain, so be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry for my daughter Hannah's husband, Richard. He's an accountant in a small firm, doing tax returns, and it sounds like the computers could do most of that. They've got three children and Hannah stays home with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Richard to look at what he's good at with people, not with numbers. I'd say Hannah and the children can come to us any time, and I'd mean it. And we'd keep the savings for them, not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be harder on office folk in public than I'd be with Richard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody marched for the mills. Would you march for the offices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. But I'd help Richard paint the house if he needed a job doing, and that's my kind of marching. You look after your own and your street. That's what we're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the grandchildren if their dad lost his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take them up to the hens and let them collect the eggs. Children don't need to hear about jobs. They need to see that Grandad still goes to work in the morning.

S2.say: I'd say it's a lot of fuss from people who sit at desks, when mill and mine workers got no march. If office workers need to retrain, so be it.
S2.think: Privately I'd worry for my son-in-law Richard, an accountant doing tax returns. They have three children and Hannah stays home with them.
S2.do: Advises Richard to focus on his skills with people and offers Hannah and the children a home if needed. Keeps the savings for them rather than for himself.
S2.feel: Uneasy, and aware he'd be harder on office workers in public than with his own son-in-law.
S2.quote: You look after your own and your street. That's what we're for.
S2.fieldNote: He's blunt in public about office workers and soft as anything about his own family. He noticed that gap himself. His idea of protest is helping paint a house, and his answer to the grandchildren is to keep going to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who got rich should do right by their communities, through their church, their town, their family, not because a government forces them. And I'd say the politicians fighting over it should be ashamed. Margaret would tell me to keep my voice down at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad to be in eggs. People will always eat eggs, rich or poor, and more of them when times are hard because they're cheap. But Richard's job would be gone by now, I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Tom if there was any extra work, weekends, deliveries to the farm shops. Margaret and I would give Hannah's family some money each month, maybe two hundred, out of the savings. And I'd cut the car back to the old one and sell the newer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't force it. What if the rich don't do it on their own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that's on their conscience. I know that sounds like nothing happens. Maybe a fair tax, a small one, on the very top, I could stand that. But not cheques for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical jobs are mostly untouched in this one. Do you feel safe at Larkfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe enough. The hens don't care who's in charge. Though I notice Tom's been reading about sheds that clean themselves, and I didn't like the look on his face.

S3.say: I'd say the people who got rich should do right by their communities through church, town and family, not because a government forces them. The politicians fighting over it should be ashamed.
S3.think: Off the record I'd be glad to be in eggs, because people eat eggs rich or poor. But Richard's job would probably be gone by now.
S3.do: Asks Tom for extra weekend or delivery work and gives Hannah's family about two hundred a month from savings. Sells the newer car and keeps the old one.
S3.quote: People will always eat eggs, rich or poor, and more of them when times are hard because they're cheap.
S3.fieldNote: His free-market instinct bent a little when pushed: a small tax on the very top he could accept, cheques for everyone he couldn't. The first sign of robot worry slipped in through Tom reading about self-cleaning sheds. Family comes first in every answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've lost our way as a country if a machine can do a man's work and we call that progress. I'd say it in church, at the pub and to Tom's face. A job is how a man keeps his dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, egg farms are already half machines. The belts bring the eggs to the grader, and I've seen sheds abroad on the television where robots roll along the floor picking up eggs the hens lay in the wrong place. I'm the one doing that by hand now, and I'm the newest man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't learn to run a robot, not at my age, I'll be straight with you. I'd ask Tom to keep me on for the jobs a machine can't do, the fox watch, the fences, the dead birds. If he couldn't, I'd look for caretaker work at the school or the church, and we'd live on Margaret's money and the savings until my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the shop closing again, but there's no new door this time. I don't want a cheque from the government for being replaced. I want a reason to put my boots on in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be straight with me and not learn the robot. What if Tom said it's that or nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it would be nothing, and I'd find something else. I'm not being stubborn. I'd be the slowest man on the course, and I'd only be keeping a young man out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Margaret say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Erik, you were miserable for a year after the shop. And she'd be right. She'd make me go to the job centre on the first Monday, before I could sit in my chair and feel sorry for myself.

S4.say: I'd say we've lost our way if a machine doing a man's work is called progress. A job is how a man keeps his dignity, and I'd say it in church, at the pub and to Tom's face.
S4.think: I think egg farms are already half machines, and robots that pick up floor eggs exist abroad. That's the job I do by hand now, and I'm the newest man.
S4.do: Asks Tom to keep him on for jobs a machine can't do, like fox watch, fences and dead birds. Otherwise looks for caretaker work at the school or church, living on Margaret's pay and savings until his pension.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like the shop closing again with no new door, and wanting a reason to work rather than a government cheque.
S4.quote: I don't want a cheque from the government for being replaced. I want a reason to put my boots on in the morning.
S4.fieldNote: Erik's resistance is principled rather than fearful: he'd step aside so a young man could take the training. Dignity, not money, is the heart of it for him. Margaret clearly knows how he takes a loss, and he admitted the shop left him miserable for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, the last one. What would help is if small farms like Tom's got help to keep people on, less paperwork and lower taxes for employing a man rather than a machine. And apprenticeships, so the young ones learn what the old ones know before we're gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When the shop shut, it was my church that got me through, not the government and not the bank. Whatever comes, people will need somewhere to go on a Sunday where nobody asks what they do for a living.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You're welcome. I have to get back, those pop-holes won't shut themselves. Not yet, anyway.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque from the government for being replaced. I want a reason to put my boots on in the morning.
portrait: Erik is a 58-year-old former hardware shop owner who now collects and grades eggs and guards the hens at dusk on a free-range egg farm. He's traditional, churchgoing and wary of handouts, and he has never used AI. In public he's blunt about office workers, but privately his worry is all for his son-in-law, an accountant with three children. With robots, he refuses to retrain, partly to leave room for a younger man, and says what he wants is work and dignity, not a cheque.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because egg farms are already half automated and he is the newest man doing the hand jobs a robot could do.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small farms to keep people on, through less paperwork and lower taxes for employing people, and real apprenticeships for the young.
